lessons.title: Reproductive anatomy of the mare and stallion
lessons.html:
The mare

The mare's reproductive tract sits in the pelvis below the rectum, which is why vets can feel the ovaries and uterus by rectal palpation.

PartFunction
VulvaExternal opening; the vulval lips form the first seal against air and dirt
Vestibule and vaginaPassage to the cervix; the vestibulo-vaginal fold is a second seal
CervixMuscular ring, the third seal; relaxes in oestrus and closes tightly in pregnancy
UterusY-shaped body and two horns; the foal develops here
OviductsWhere fertilisation takes place
OvariesBean-shaped; produce eggs (ova) and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. In the mare, ovulation happens at the ovulation fossa.

Poor vulval conformation, common in older or thin mares, lets air and faeces into the vagina (windsucking) and causes infections. A vet may perform a Caslick's procedure to close the upper vulva.

The stallion

PartFunction
TestesProduce sperm and testosterone; held in the scrotum, cooler than body temperature
EpididymisStores and matures sperm
Vas deferensCarries sperm to the urethra
Accessory glandsSeminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands add fluid to form semen
Penis and prepuce (sheath)Deposits semen; the sheath protects the penis

A colt with one or both testes not descended into the scrotum is a rig (cryptorchid). He may still behave like a stallion and should be examined by a vet.

The oestrous cycle

Mares are seasonal, long-day breeders: they cycle when days are long, roughly spring and summer (about September to February in South Africa). The cycle lasts about 21 days, of which oestrus (heat) lasts about 5 to 7 days. Ovulation usually happens towards the end of oestrus. Breeders of racehorses often use artificial lighting from winter to start cycling earlier, because all Thoroughbreds in South Africa share an official birthday.

lessons.title: Gestation and pregnancy diagnosis
lessons.html:
Gestation parameters

Gestation in the mare averages about 340 days (about 11 months), but a normal range is roughly 320 to 365 days. Gestation tends to be longer for colts and for mares foaling early in the season. A foal born well before about 320 days is premature and needs vet care.

Stages of pregnancy

  • Early (first trimester): the embryo enters the uterus at about day 6 and moves around the uterus until about day 16, when it fixes in position. Endometrial cups form around day 35 to 40 and produce the hormone eCG.
  • Mid-pregnancy: the foetus grows slowly; organs develop.
  • Late (last trimester): most foetal growth happens now, so the mare's feed requirements rise sharply.

Techniques for pregnancy diagnosis

MethodTiming and notes
TeasingMare refuses the stallion 16 to 21 days after service. Simple but unreliable on its own.
Ultrasound scanning (rectal)By a vet from about 14 to 16 days. Detects twins early, the most important check.
Rectal palpationBy a vet from about 25 to 30 days onward.
Blood testseCG test from about day 40 to 120; oestrogen tests in later pregnancy.

Why twins matter

Twin pregnancies in mares usually end in abortion or weak foals. The vet scans early, around day 14 to 16, and if twins are found, pinches out one embryo so that a single pregnancy continues. This is why the early scan is standard practice on stud farms. A second scan at about 25 to 30 days confirms a heartbeat, and later checks catch early embryonic loss.

lessons.title: Health care for the pregnant mare
lessons.html:
A health-care programme for the pregnant mare

Plan the programme with the stud vet and record every action in the mare's file.

Nutrition

  • Early and mid-pregnancy: maintain a body condition score of about moderate to fleshy. Good grazing or hay is usually enough.
  • Last trimester: increase energy, protein, calcium and phosphorus as the foetus grows fast. Use a balanced stud ration as advised.
  • Avoid sudden changes, mouldy feed and obesity, which increase foaling problems.
  • Fresh water always.

Vaccination and deworming

  • Follow the vet's vaccination schedule. Some vaccines are given in late pregnancy so that the colostrum is rich in antibodies.
  • Use only dewormers that the label states are safe for pregnant mares; base deworming on faecal egg counts.
  • African horse sickness vaccination must follow the vet's advice on timing in pregnant mares.

Exercise, hooves and teeth

  • Daily turnout for gentle exercise.
  • Regular farrier visits and dental checks.

Monitoring

  • Watch for vaginal discharge, early udder development or milk dripping long before term; these may signal placentitis or abortion risk. Call the vet.
  • About a month before foaling, move the mare to the foaling camp so she builds immunity to local germs.
  • Signs of approaching birth: udder filling, waxing of teats, relaxed muscles around the tail head.

Key points

  • The cervix and vulva form seals that protect the uterus.
  • Mares are long-day breeders with a cycle of about 21 days.
  • Average gestation is about 340 days, normal range about 320 to 365.
  • Scan early (day 14 to 16) to detect and manage twins.
  • Feed requirements rise sharply in the last trimester.
  • Report discharge or early udder development to the vet.
